answer: Yes, several people did, and some of the arguments are still going. The best-known rival was Elisha Gray. He filed a patent caveat (a notice that he planned to file a patent) for a very similar device on February 14, 1876, the same day as Bell's application but a few hours later. The dispute went to court, and Bell won [1][2]. Antonio Meucci, an Italian immigrant in New York, filed a caveat for a "sound telegraph" in 1871 but couldn't afford the fee to keep it active. In 2002 the U.S. House passed Resolution 269, which recognized his work and is often read as crediting him first [1]. Historians point out that his caveat didn't describe sending a voice, and there's no evidence that Bell copied him [1]. Others worked on the same idea around that time, including the German inventor Johann Philipp Reis. Bell's patents held up through a long series of lawsuits known as the Telephone Cases [2][3].
